827.title: The fish who prayed for rain
827.hook: a fish king makes the rain fall by an act of truth (Jataka 75)
827.howItsDone: The act of truth appears elsewhere in the Pali texts too: in the Angulimala Sutta, Angulimala speaks a true sentence about his own life as a blessing for a woman in labor, and those words are chanted as a protective verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the virtuous elephant, sila itself, who carried a lost man home and then watched him come back with a saw. Your line was good to the ungrateful. Was there an ingratitude you let go? Today, a new week, and a drought. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

Cracked mud, in plates, where the water used to be. Each day the edge pulls back a little further. The fish crowd into what's left, and the crows and herons have noticed. They stand at the edge, waiting. In this Jataka tale, the Buddha in an earlier life is one of those fish, the king of the pond. He can't fly away. He can't dig a well. He has one thing left to offer, and it isn't a plea or a bargain. It's a sentence that happens to be true. Today, the fish who prayed for rain.
screen: `THE MUD CRACKS INTO PLATES.` → `THE HERONS ARE WAITING.` → `ONE THING LEFT TO OFFER.`

segments.voice: First, the drought. The tale sets it in the kingdom of Kosala. No rain comes, the crops wither, and the pond goes to mud. The fish are stuck, and the birds are picking them off one by one. Second, the fish king rises. He pushes up out of the mud, looks at the sky, and calls on Pajjunna, the god of the rain clouds in the story. But he doesn't ask for a favor. Third, the act of truth. In Pali it's called sacca-kiriya. A person states something true about their own life, sets it out like an offering, and the truth itself carries power. The fish king's truth is this: though he was born among fish, who eat one another, he has never, as far back as he can remember, taken the life of any creature. If that is true, he says, let the rain fall. And it does. The clouds gather, the pond fills, and the fish are saved. Fourth, why it matters. The act of truth only works because it's true. The fish can't bluff the sky. Whatever power his words have comes from the life standing behind them. That's the part worth keeping. He doesn't promise to be good from now on. He doesn't describe the kind of fish he hopes to be. He points to what he has already done, plainly, and lets it speak. Some readers hear a quiet question in the tale for anyone listening: what could you say about your own life that's simply true? Not impressive. Not polished. Just true enough to stand on.
screen: `A POND GOING DRY.` · `HE CALLS ON THE RAIN-GOD.` · `NOT A FAVOR: A TRUTH.` · `THE RAIN COMES.` · then, large: `AN ACT OF TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one true thing aloud. First, settle. Feel the breath come in and go out a few times. Then look for something about your life that's plainly true. It doesn't need to be grand. I kept a promise this week. I'm tired today. I love my brother. When you find it, say it out loud, quietly, just once. Then sit with how it sounds in the room. Is it solid? Does it need anything added? The fish king had one true sentence, and the sky answered. Yours only has to be true. The bell holds the time.
Sacca-kiriya. An act of truth: a fish king in a dying pond speaks one plain truth about his life, and the rain falls. Today's word.
Your line: an act of truth. Today, before you make a promise or a claim, ask whether it could stand as an act of truth: plain, sure, and yours. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

options: burrow deep and wait it out.
rise up and speak one true thing to the sky.
lead the fish toward the far bank.
fork.reveal: he calls on the rain-god with an act of truth: he has never taken a life. the rain falls and fills the pond.

original.note: Pali: sacca-kiriya, an act of truth; sacca is truth, kiriya an act.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable about a fish who got lucky with the weather.
what it means: the fish king offers a true statement about his own life, and the truth brings the rain.
what a scholar hears: the act of truth, sacca-kiriya, also appears in other Pali texts, such as the Angulimala Sutta.

828.title: The forest of ogresses
828.hook: a prince crosses a forest of temptations without looking back (Jataka 96)
828.howItsDone: In Buddhist practice this is called guarding the sense doors: noticing a sight or a sound without being pulled after it, trained in both walking and sitting meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a fish king in a dry pond spoke his sacca-kiriya, one true sentence, and the rain came. Your line was an act of truth. Did you say something plainly true? Today, a road through a dangerous forest. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

The road to the throne runs straight through a forest, and the forest is not empty. Along the way, the tale says, ogresses wait, and they don't look like monsters. They build pleasant houses by the road, spread soft couches, and call out sweetly to anyone passing. A young prince sets out to cross it anyway, because holy men have told him one thing: keep walking, and don't look at them. Today, the forest of ogresses.
screen: `A ROAD THROUGH THE FOREST.` → `LOVELY HOUSES, SOFT COUCHES.` → `KEEP WALKING. DON'T LOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the warning. Before he leaves, the prince is told that the ogresses will tempt travelers through every door of the senses: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touch. Whoever stops to look is lost. Second, the companions. A few men insist on coming with him, sure they can manage. One by one they fall behind. One stops for a lovely form, one for a song, one for a sweet scent, one for a fine meal, one for a soft bed. The ogresses take each of them. Third, the one who follows. The prince walks on alone. One ogress won't give up. She follows him all the way to the city, telling everyone she meets that she's his wife. He never so much as glances at her. She ends up in the king's palace, and the story turns dark for the king who took her in. The prince, who never turned his head, ends up on the throne. Fourth, the bowl of oil. The tale is called the Telapatta Jataka, the bowl-of-oil birth story, and it's linked to a teaching in the Samyutta Nikaya. There, a man must carry a bowl filled to the brim with oil through a crowd watching a famous beauty dance, while a man with a drawn sword walks behind him, ready to strike if a drop spills. The Buddha says the bowl stands for mindfulness of the body. Both stories make the same point. The trouble isn't that the lure is there. It's turning toward it. Attention is where the danger lies, and where the protection lies too.
screen: `THE WARNING: DON'T LOOK.` · `COMPANIONS FALL ONE BY ONE.` · `ONE FOLLOWS HIM TO THE CITY.` · `A BOWL OF OIL, FULL TO THE BRIM.` · then, large: `DON'T LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, and let something tempt you. It will. A phone face down nearby, a snack in the kitchen, a plan for tomorrow. When it calls, notice it: the picture, the sound, the pull. Then don't turn your head. Come back to the breath, like the man carrying the oil, steady and full. You can know the lure is there and still walk past it. Later today, choose one temptation and walk past it, once. The bell holds the time.
Yakkhini. A female yakkha, an ogress of the wild places: what filled the forest a prince crossed by keeping his eyes on the road, while those who stopped to look were lost. Today's word.
Your line: don't look back. Today, when something pulls at your attention, keep walking once, and see what it's like on the other side. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scary story about monsters in the woods.
what it means: the lures come through the senses; whoever stops for each one is lost, and the one who keeps walking gets through.
what a scholar hears: the tale is named Telapatta, bowl of oil, and is linked to the sutta of a man carrying a brimming bowl past a crowd, a picture of mindfulness of the body.

829.title: The tiger raised
829.hook: a student with a spell revives a dead tiger, which kills him (Jataka 150)
829.tomorrow: The donkey in the lion's skin
829.howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold in Buddhist sermons and children's classes, and a retelling often closes on the tale's verse, here the teacher's warning about whom we help back to their feet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prince walked through a forest of yakkhini, without turning his head. Your line was don't look back. Did you walk past something? Today, a spell, and a tiger. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

A spell for raising the dead. That's what a young student named Sanjiva has picked up from his teacher. Only half of it, though: the words that bring a body back to life, and not the words that would undo them. One day he's out in the forest with the other students, gathering wood, and they come across a dead tiger lying in the grass. Sanjiva has an idea. His friends have a different one. Today, the tiger raised.
screen: `HALF A SPELL.` → `A DEAD TIGER IN THE GRASS.` → `SANJIVA HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: First, the half-learned spell. The tale says Sanjiva knew the charm for raising the dead but had never learned the charm for putting them down again. He has the start of something and no way to finish it. Second, the boast. He tells his friends he'll bring the tiger back to life. They don't quite believe him, but they aren't foolish either. Before he begins, they climb up into the trees. Third, the waking. Sanjiva says the words. The tiger stirs, rises, and the first thing it does is spring at the man who woke it. It kills him on the spot, and the tale says the tiger fell dead right there beside him. His friends come down from the branches and carry the news home. Fourth, the teacher's verse. The teacher, the Buddha in an earlier life, hears what happened and gives the tale its lesson: whoever helps a wicked one back to his feet is harmed by him, just as the tiger killed the one who raised it. The frame of the story is about a king who took a schemer as his friend, so the warning first of all concerns companions. But the picture reaches further than that. Some things in a life are lying still for good reason: an old grudge, a habit that nearly sank you, an argument that finally went quiet. The words that wake them are easy to say. Putting them down again is the half of the spell that's easy to skip.
screen: `HALF A SPELL.` · `FRIENDS CLIMB THE TREES.` · `THE TIGER WAKES AND SPRINGS.` · `DON'T RAISE THE WICKED.` · then, large: `CAREFUL WHAT YOU REVIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, and let the mind wander a little, and watch what it tries to wake. An old argument. A grudge. A craving that had gone quiet. You'll know it when it stirs. Don't say the words that bring it to its feet. See it lying there, and leave it in the grass. Come back to the breath. Later today, before you reopen something that's been still, pause once and ask: do I know how to put this down again? The bell holds the time.
Sanjiva. The student with half a spell, who revived a dead tiger in a Jataka tale, and was killed by it. Today's word.
Your line: careful what you revive. Today, before you bring back an old quarrel or an old habit, ask whether you know the other half of the spell. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

screen: `DAY 829 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DONKEY IN THE LION'S SKIN.`

830.title: The donkey in the lion's skin
830.hook: a donkey in a lion's skin is fine until he brays (Jataka 189)
830.howItsDone: In the Pali Canon, the Jataka's verses are the scripture and the prose stories come from the commentary told around them, so a retelling of this tale builds toward its verse about the bray.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sanjiva and the tiger he woke with half a spell. Your line was careful what you revive. Did you leave something lying still? Today, a disguise in a barley field. Day eight hundred thirty.

There's a lion in the barley field. Or there seems to be. The watchmen see the tawny hide from the edge of the field and back away. Every day it's there again, head down, eating the crop, and every day nobody dares go near it. The crop gets thinner, row by row, and still nobody goes closer. Nobody stops to wonder about one small thing. Odd, for a lion, to eat barley. Today, the donkey in the lion's skin.
screen: `A LION IN THE BARLEY.` → `THE WATCHMEN BACK AWAY.` → `ODD, FOR A LION, TO EAT BARLEY.`

segments.voice: First, the trick. A traveling merchant carries his goods from village to village on a donkey. At each stop he unloads, throws a lion's skin over the donkey, and turns it loose in the fields. The watchmen take it for a lion and keep their distance, and the donkey eats well. Second, the village rises. At one village, the watchmen decide they've had enough. They rouse the people, and out they come with drums and conch shells, shouting, heading for the field together. Third, the bray. Terrified by the noise, the donkey does the one thing a donkey can do. It brays. And the game is over. The villagers know a bray when they hear one. They fall on the donkey, and in the tale it is beaten to death in the field. The verse sums it up, in words close to these: that's no lion's roar, no tiger's, no panther's; it's a wretched donkey in a lion's skin. Fourth, what the tale is about. The skin worked. From a distance it fooled everyone. What gave the donkey away wasn't how it looked. It was its own voice, the moment fear pressed on it. Under pressure, what we are comes out, whatever we're wearing. Some readers add that the trouble was never being a donkey. A donkey is a useful, honest thing to be. It carries the load. The trouble only started when it had to pass for a lion, and keep passing, until the day the drums came.
screen: `A LION'S SKIN ON A DONKEY.` · `THE VILLAGE COMES WITH DRUMS.` · `THE DONKEY BRAYS.` · `A DONKEY IS FINE TO BE.` · then, large: `THE BRAY GIVES IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit as you actually are today. Not the version for work, or for photos, or for a camera. Find the posture you'd take if no one were looking, and take it. Let the breath go at its own pace, not a calm one you're performing. If a thought comes about how you seem, let it pass by. For these two minutes, there's no skin to hold up. The bell holds the time.
Siha. Lion: the name in the tale of a donkey's borrowed hide that fools the watchmen, until the drums come and the donkey brays. Today's word.
Your line: the bray gives it away. Today, notice one place where you're wearing a skin, and try being what you are, just there, just once. Day eight hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 830 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOODPECKER AND THE LION.`

trapdoor: what you thought: a joke about a silly donkey.
what it means: a borrowed image holds until pressure brings out the real voice.
what a scholar hears: the Pali name is Sihacamma, lion's skin, and the tale's verse turns on the bray: no lion's roar, but a donkey's.

831.title: The woodpecker and the lion
831.hook: a woodpecker frees a bone from a lion's throat; the lion won't share (Jataka 308)
831.howItsDone: The Anguttara Nikaya names two kinds of people hard to find in the world: one who does a kindness first, and one who is grateful for it. In this tale the woodpecker is the first, and the lion is not the second.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a donkey in a lion's skin, a siha's skin, gave itself away with one bray. Your line was the bray gives it away. Where were you simply what you are? Today, a real lion, and a very small bird. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

A lion lies in the forest and can't eat. While he was gulping down his kill, a bone lodged in his throat, and now his throat is swelling and the pain won't stop. A woodpecker on a branch above sees him suffering and flutters down to ask what's wrong. What is a bird supposed to do about a lion's throat? Quite a lot, it turns out. Today, the woodpecker and the lion.
screen: `A BONE IN A LION'S THROAT.` → `A WOODPECKER ON A BRANCH.` → `WHAT CAN A BIRD DO?`

segments.voice: First, the stick. The woodpecker wants to help, but he isn't careless about it. He knows a lion's mouth is no place to be. So he takes a stick and props the lion's jaws wide open. Only then does he go in, and with his beak he knocks the bone loose. He comes back out and knocks the stick away. Second, the hungry day. Some time later the woodpecker can find nothing to eat. He comes across the lion feasting on a fresh kill, and he asks, politely, for a little share. Third, the lion's answer. No. You've been inside a lion's mouth, the lion says, and come out alive. Let that be payment enough. Fourth, what the bird does next. A spirit living in a nearby tree asks the woodpecker why he doesn't strike back. He could peck at the lion's eyes. The woodpecker says no. Nothing good comes of harming someone who doesn't know what he owes. He'll simply go. And he flies off. A few days back, the elephant was good to a man who repaid him with a saw. This tale asks a smaller, more everyday question: what about help that's just never thanked? The woodpecker shows two things. Help wisely, with a stick in the jaws, so your kindness doesn't get you eaten. And don't turn the help into a bill. Once it's given, it's given. He's still hungry when he flies away, and still free.
screen: `A STICK PROPS THE JAWS OPEN.` · `THE BIRD ASKS FOR A SHARE.` · `THE LION WON'T SHARE.` · `NO REVENGE. HE FLIES OFF.` · then, large: `HELP ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one help, the woodpecker's way. Bring to mind someone who could use a hand this week. First, find your stick: the one sensible precaution that keeps the help from costing more than you can give. A set time, a clear limit, a question asked first. Then, before you've even done it, close the account in advance. No thanks expected, no share owed. Breathe with that for a while. Later today, give the help, and don't mention it. The bell holds the time.
Strike back. What the woodpecker wouldn't do to the lion who wouldn't share his meal, after freeing a bone from its throat, choosing instead to simply fly off. Today's word.
Your line: help anyway. Today, help someone once, wisely, and let the thanks be optional. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: The preacher of patience
832.hook: an ascetic stays patient while a drunken king has his limbs cut (Jataka 313)
832.howItsDone: Patience, khanti, is one of the ten perfections in the Theravada tradition, and this tale is told as the Bodhisatta's practice of that perfection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woodpecker freed a lion's throat and flew off, no strike back. Your line was help anyway. Did you help without keeping the bill? Today, a hard tale, and a steady man at its center. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

A king falls asleep in his pleasure garden, drunk, with his head in the lap of one of his women. The women of his court, bored with waiting, wander off through the trees and find an ascetic sitting quietly by himself. They sit down around him and ask him to teach. When the king wakes and finds them gone, he goes looking for them, and he is furious. A word of warning: this tale has violence in it, and it's told plainly. Today, the preacher of patience.
screen: `A KING ASLEEP, DRUNK.` → `HIS WOMEN FIND AN ASCETIC.` → `THE KING WAKES, FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The king demands to know what this ascetic teaches. Patience, he answers. In Pali, khanti. That's why the tale calls him Khantivadi, the preacher of patience. Second, the test. The king calls for his executioner. He has the ascetic flogged, and then, one cruelty after another, has his hands and feet cut off, then his ears and nose. After each one the king asks him: what do you teach now? And each time the answer is the same. Third, where patience lives. The ascetic tells the king that his patience isn't in his hands or his feet, or in any part of him a blade can reach. It lies deep within, in the heart. The king kicks him and walks away. And in the tale, as the king leaves the garden, the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the last word. The king's commander comes back to the dying man and begs him: if you must be angry, be angry with the king, not with the kingdom. The ascetic answers that he wishes the king long life, and that people like him do not get angry. Then he dies. The tale is very hard to hear, and it isn't advice to stay where you're being harmed. It's a picture of a quality pushed to its far edge: patience that doesn't live anywhere the world can cut. What tests an ordinary day is far smaller. A slow line, a loud neighbor, a careless remark. That's where the practicing happens.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU TEACH? PATIENCE.` · `THE KING TESTS IT.` · `NOT IN HANDS OR FEET.` · `MAY THE KING LIVE LONG.` · then, large: `PATIENCE HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a small one: stay patient in one irritation. Sit, and wait for one to arrive. It might be a sound outside, an itch, a thought that you're wasting time. When it comes, don't fix it. Feel where it pinches, and breathe toward that spot. See whether the patience lives in the itch, or somewhere further in. Later today, when one small thing grates, give it three breaths before you answer. The bell holds the time.
Khanti. Patience: what an ascetic named for it keeps while a drunken king cuts him down, and wishes the king long life. Today's word.
Your line: patience holds. Today, give one irritation three breaths before you answer it. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

what it means: patience that lives deep within can't be cut away, whatever happens to the body.
what a scholar hears: the ascetic's name, Khantivadi, means the preacher of patience, and the tale is read as the perfection of patience, khanti.

833.title: The sky is falling
833.hook: a hare hears a fruit fall and starts a stampede; a lion checks the facts (Jataka 322)
833.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching on right speech asks whether words are true, helpful and timely before they're spoken, and teachers sometimes use this tale to show how a rumor grows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the preacher of khanti, patience, whose patience no blade could reach. Your line was patience holds. Did one irritation get its three breaths? Today, a noise in the forest. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

Thud. A hare is lying under a palm tree, near a grove of vilva trees, turning over an anxious thought: if the earth broke apart, what would become of me? Just then a ripe vilva fruit drops onto a dry palm leaf right beside him. Thud. He doesn't look round to see what it was. He's already running, and shouting as he goes. The old saying has the sky falling. In this Jataka tale, it's the earth. Today, the sky is falling.
screen: `AN ANXIOUS HARE.` → `A FRUIT DROPS ON A LEAF.` → `HE RUNS WITHOUT LOOKING.`

segments.voice: First, the run. The hare cries that the earth is breaking up. Another hare sees him running and runs too, without asking why. Then more hares join, then deer and boars, buffaloes and tigers, even elephants, a whole forest pounding along together, heading for the sea. Second, the lion. A lion sees the stampede and asks the one question nobody has asked: who saw the earth breaking up? The elephants don't know; the tigers told them. The tigers point to others, and so on down the line, until it comes back to the hares, and the hares point at one hare. Third, the check. The lion turns to that hare. Where were you when you heard it? The lion takes the hare on his back and goes to the spot. There's the palm leaf. There's the fruit lying on it. Fourth, the return. The lion goes back to the herd and tells them what he found, and the animals, who were running toward the sea, are saved. In the tale the lion is the Buddha in an earlier life, and his gift is not strength or speed. One question, and the patience to walk back and look. A frightening thing passes from mouth to mouth and grows as it goes. Everyone runs because someone else is running. Nobody goes back to the palm leaf.
screen: `THE WHOLE FOREST RUNS.` · `WHO SAW IT?` · `BACK TO THE PALM LEAF.` · `THE HERD IS SAVED.` · then, large: `CHECK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, and let the mind bring up one worry it's picked up from somewhere. Something passed along, half-heard, shared without a source. Watch how fast it wants to run. Then ask the lion's question: who saw it? Where's the palm leaf? You don't need an answer now. Just feel the difference between a thud and a falling world. Later today, check one rumor before you pass it on. The bell holds the time.
Palm leaf. What a lion found at the bottom of a rumor, a hare's fruit fallen onto a dry palm leaf, after the whole forest stampeded toward the sea. Today's word.

Your line: check first. Today, before you share something alarming, go find the palm leaf. And look back at this week's lines: an act of truth, don't look back, careful what you revive, the bray gives it away, help anyway, patience holds, and now check first. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

match.prompt: the hare and the lion: tap the pairs.

myth: in the Jataka the hare cries that the sky is falling
the hare cries that the earth is breaking up.
the lion carried the hare back to the spot
and there was the palm leaf, with the fruit lying on it.
the elephants started the panic
it began with one hare and spread all the way up to the elephants.

fork.setup: you're the lion, and the whole forest is stampeding past you toward the sea. what do you do?
options: run with them; they must know something.
ask who saw it, and go back to look.
roar to make them run faster.
fork.reveal: the lion traces the story back to one hare, carries him to the spot, finds the fruit on the palm leaf, and saves the herd.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nursery tale about panic.
what it means: one unchecked sound becomes a stampede, and one question stops it.
what a scholar hears: in the Jataka the hare fears the earth breaking up, not the sky, and the lion who checks is the Bodhisatta.
